THOUGHT: This 17-year-old sexually active female presents with a 5-day history of severe lower abdominal pain, cramping, nausea, vomiting, dysuria, and dyspareunia. Key clinical features include fever (38.5°C), generalized lower abdominal tenderness (more pronounced in lower quadrants), cervical motion tenderness on pelvic exam, and purulent cervical discharge — all highly suggestive of upper genital tract infection. Her elevated WBC (15,000/mm³) and markedly elevated ESR (100 mm/h) indicate significant systemic inflammation. Inconsistent condom use increases risk for sexually transmitted infections (STIs). While dysuria and burning with intercourse raise concern for lower urinary tract or vaginal infection, the presence of cervical motion tenderness — a classic sign of pelvic inflammatory disease (PID) — along with systemic signs (fever, leukocytosis, elevated ESR) and purulent discharge strongly points to PID rather than uncomplicated cystitis, vaginitis, or cervicitis alone. The absence of reported urinary frequency/urgency makes simple UTI less likely. Pregnancy status is unknown but must be ruled out; however, even if pregnant, PID remains the leading diagnosis given the constellation of findings — and PID can occur regardless of pregnancy status. Other considerations (e.g., appendicitis, ectopic pregnancy, ovarian torsion) are less likely: no right-lower-quadrant predominance or peritoneal signs suggesting appendicitis; no amenorrhea or positive pregnancy test to support ectopic; no acute unilateral adnexal mass or sudden onset typical of torsion. CDC criteria for empirical PID diagnosis include: lower abdominal pain + cervical motion tenderness *or* uterine/adnexal tenderness + one or more of: fever >38.0°C, purulent cervical/vaginal discharge, elevated WBC/ESR, or lab-confirmed gonorrhea/chlamydia. This patient meets multiple criteria — thus, PID is the most likely diagnosis.

DIAGNOSIS: Pelvic Inflammatory Disease
